Assume \(p,q>0\) (the usual case for this statement). Let

\[
a\in H^p(S^p)\cong \mathbb Z,\qquad b\in H^q(S^q)\cong \mathbb Z
\]

be generators, and let

\[
\alpha=\pi_1^*a\in H^p(S^p\times S^q),\qquad 
\beta=\pi_2^*b\in H^q(S^p\times S^q).
\]

By the Künneth theorem,

\[
H^n(S^p\times S^q)\cong H^{p+q}(S^p\times S^q)
\]

is generated by the cup product \(\alpha\smile \beta\).

Since \(0<p<n\) and \(0<q<n\), the cohomology groups of \(S^n\) vanish in those intermediate degrees:

\[
H^p(S^n)=0,\qquad H^q(S^n)=0.
\]

Hence

\[
f^*\alpha=0\in H^p(S^n),\qquad f^*\beta=0\in H^q(S^n).
\]

Because \(f^*\) is a ring homomorphism,

\[
f^*(\alpha\smile \beta)
=
f^*\alpha \smile f^*\beta
=
0\smile 0
=
0.
\]

Thus \(f^*\) sends a generator of \(H^n(S^p\times S^q)\) to \(0\), so the whole induced map is zero:

\[
\boxed{f^*=0: H^n(S^p\times S^q)\to H^n(S^n)}
\]

If one allows \(p=0\) or \(q=0\), then \(S^0\times S^n\) is disconnected and the map depends on which component \(f\) lands in and on the degree of the resulting map \(S^n\to S^n\); in the standard positive-dimensional case the answer is the zero map.
